newsitem.title: USA: Clinton turns attention to economic appointments.
newsitem.headline: Clinton turns attention to economic appointments.

text.p: Having selected his foreign policy team, President Bill Clinton turns his attention this week to the domestic front, honing in on the administration's key economic jobs.

At the very top there is little uncertainty, with U.S. officials saying there is no doubt U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will stay on. Rubin himself, appearing on NBC's "Meet the Press" programme on Sunday, wryly remarked, "I think you'll likely see a relatively familiar face at Treasury."
Administration officials also said that Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers has indicated he wishes to remain in his job and was expected to do so.
Beyond those two, a host of other jobs are up in the air, including the chairman of the National Economic Council (NEC) and the secretaries of commerce and labour.
The NEC, a Clinton innovation, was created to coordinate administration economic policy and to hammer out disputes within the government. As its first chairman, Rubin played an influential role.
The current chair, Laura Tyson, has indicated she wants to leave to teach at the University of California at Berkeley.

Newspaper reports have suggested Clinton may name two people to replace Tyson: Gene Sperling, her deputy, and Daniel Tarullo, the White House "sherpa" who prepares U.S. positions for Group of Seven (G7) summits.

One U.S. official who declined to be identified said there was debate within the administration about whether this was a good idea, saying there was concern that to split the job would be to diminish it.

However, another official said if the administration could come to a consensus on this, it was possible the two men would run the council jointly, with Sperling taking the lead on domestic matters and Tarullo on international subjects.

After Clinton named U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright to be secretary of state and Republican Sen. William Cohen as his nominee for secretary of defence on last Thursday, Erskine Bowles, the incoming White House chief of staff, said he himself was open to the idea of two people sharing the NEC chairman's job.

However, another U.S. official said the White House was also considering other options -- with Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat cited as one possibility and former deputy U.S. Trade Representative Rufus Yerxa as another.
Eizenstat served at the White House as former President Jimmy Carter's top domestic policy adviser from 1977 to 1981.

One official said there are several names circulating as possible nominees for secretaries of commerce and labour. Two people cited for labour secretary are Alexis Herman, director of public liaison at the White House, and William Daley, the brother of Chicago Mayor Richard Daley.

Daley is also in the running for commerce secretary, as is Representative Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat who has led a series of missions to rescue U.S. citizens detained abroad. Richardson is also said to be a candidate for U.N. ambassador.
One administration official said Clinton has told Charlene Barshefsky, the acting U.S. trade representative, that he will do whatevery he can to keep her in that position.

Barshefsky got the job when Mickey Kantor succeeded the late Ron Brown as commerce secretary, but she has not been confirmed, partly because of concerns about work she did as a private lawyer in advising Canada on a lumber dispute.

One official referred to the matter as a "legislative" issue, saying the White House was working with Congress to seek Senate confirmation for Barshefsky and that it was hopeful it could be worked out.

Noting that Clinton took his time choosing his national security team, officials were loath to predict when he may make an announcement on the economic team, with one saying that late this week was a possibility.
